L0: # API keys
L1: 
L2: Use API keys to authenticate API requests.
L3: 
L4: Read this page in your terminal: [install the Stripe CLI](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/install) (v1.43.3+) and run `stripe docs`. [Reference](https://docs.stripe.com/cli/docs)
L5: ## Start here: Integrate with Stripe using skills and plugins
L6: 
L7: Stripe provides skills and plugins for agents to build faster and more accurately. See [Agent skills](https://docs.stripe.com/skills.md) for more information.
L8: 
L9: **Quickstart**: Install the Stripe CLI with `npm install -g @stripe/cli` and run `stripe agent setup`.
L10: Stripe uses API keys to authenticate requests from your integration and determine which Stripe resources it can access. Choose the key type that matches where your code runs and grant server-side keys only the permissions your integration needs.
L11: Use the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys) page in the Dashboard to create, reveal, expire, and rotate keys for the account or sandbox you’re viewing. This guide covers keys used with the Stripe API. To learn about API v2 endpoints, behavior, and testing, see the [API v2 overview](https://docs.stripe.com/api-v2-overview.md).
L12: If a request doesn’t include a valid key, Stripe returns an [invalid request error](https://docs.stripe.com/error-handling.md#invalid-request-errors). If a request includes an expired key, Stripe returns an [authentication error](https://docs.stripe.com/error-handling.md#authentication-errors). Use [Workbench request logs](https://docs.stripe.com/workbench.md) to inspect API requests and troubleshoot errors.
L13: > #### If you're new to Stripe
L14: >
L15: > - **Keep your business safe:** Read our [best practices](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md) for managing keys.
L16: - **Build and test**: Create or select a [sandbox](https://docs.stripe.com/sandboxes.md) and use its test keys. For new integrations, use a separate general sandbox instead of your account’s test mode sandbox so settings and data remain isolated from live mode. Sandbox keys start with `pk_test_` for publishable keys, `rk_test_` for restricted keys, and `sk_test_` for secret keys.
L17: - **When you’re ready to accept real payments**: [Switch to your live mode keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#switch-to-live-mode), which start with `pk_live_`, `rk_live_`, and `sk_live_`.
L18: - **If you need to find a webhook signing secret**: Webhook secrets are separate from API keys. Find them in the [Webhooks](https://dashboard.stripe.com/webhooks) section of the Dashboard under each webhook endpoint.
L19: ## Key types
L20: 
L21: When you sign up for a Stripe account, we create three types of API keys for you:
L22: | Type | Safe to expose | Description |
L23: | --- | --- | --- |
L24: | Publishable API key `pk_...` | Yes | API key for Stripe.js, Elements, and mobile SDKs. It can identify your account and create tokens or PaymentMethods from payment details, but it can’t perform sensitive operations such as creating charges or reading account data. You can include it in front-end code or applications you distribute. |
L25: | Restricted API key (RAK) `rk_...` | No | API key with permissions you control. Limit the damage to your business that a fraudulent actor could cause if they obtained your key. Create as many RAKs as you want and assign them to different parts of your application. Stripe Apps can also use [RAK authentication](https://docs.stripe.com/stripe-apps/api-authentication/rak.md) to generate a permissioned key when a user installs an app.
L26: [This guide](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/restricted-api-keys.md) explains how to configure and use RAKs. |
L27: | Secret API key `sk_...` | No | API key that has unrestricted permissions on all Stripe APIs. Because you can’t limit their permissions, we don’t recommend using secret keys for new use cases, and for existing integrations, we recommend migrating secret key usage to RAKs. |
L28: | Organization API key `sk_org_...` | No | API key that works at the organization level. Same as account-level restricted or secret keys, but operates at the [organization](https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/account/orgs.md) level to manage multiple Stripe accounts at once. [This guide](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/organization-api-keys.md) explains how to configure and use organization API keys. |
L29: We also support [managed API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/managed-api-keys.md) issued by certain hosting platforms. Managed keys are secret API keys that a hosting platform delivers directly to your hosted applications. You don’t need to handle managed keys directly; your hosting provider issues and rotates them for you.
L30: > #### Webhook signing secrets
L31: >
L32: > Webhook signing secrets aren’t API keys—they’re per-webhook secrets that your webhook receiver uses to authenticate that webhooks actually came from Stripe. You can find the signing secret for each webhook endpoint in the [Webhooks](https://dashboard.stripe.com/webhooks) section of the Dashboard.
L33: 
L34: You’re responsible for managing your API keys safely. Read our guide to [best practices for protecting API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md).
L35: ### Sandbox versus live mode
L36: All Stripe API requests occur in either a *sandbox* (A sandbox is an isolated test environment that allows you to test Stripe functionality in your account without affecting your live integration. Use sandboxes to safely experiment with new features and changes) or *live mode* (Use this mode when you’re ready to launch your app. Card networks or payment providers process payments). You can use a sandbox to test your integration and access test data, and live mode to access actual account data.
L37: Each mode has its own set of API keys, and objects in one mode aren’t accessible to the other. For example, a sandbox [product object](https://docs.stripe.com/api/products/object.md) can’t be part of a live mode payment.
L38: | Type | When to use | Objects | How to use | Considerations |
L39: | --- | --- | --- | --- | --- |
L40: | Sandboxes | Use a sandbox, and its associated test API keys, as you build your integration. In a sandbox, card networks and payment providers don’t process payments. | API calls return simulated objects.
L41: For example, you can retrieve and use test [Customer](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customers/object.md), [PaymentIntent](https://docs.stripe.com/api/payment_intents/object.md), [Refund](https://docs.stripe.com/api/refunds/object.md), and [Subscription](https://docs.stripe.com/api/subscriptions/object.md) objects. | Use [test credit cards and accounts](https://docs.stripe.com/testing.md#cards). You can’t accept real payment methods or work with real accounts.
L42: | [Identity](https://docs.stripe.com/identity.md) doesn’t perform any verification checks. Also, Connect [account objects](https://docs.stripe.com/api/accounts/object.md) don’t return sensitive fields. |
L43: | Live mode | Use live mode, and its associated live API keys, when you’re ready to launch your integration and accept real money. In live mode, card networks and payment providers do process payments. | API calls return real objects.
L44: For example, you can retrieve and use real [Customer](https://docs.stripe.com/api/customers/object.md), [PaymentIntent](https://docs.stripe.com/api/payment_intents/object.md), [Refund](https://docs.stripe.com/api/refunds/object.md), and [Subscription](https://docs.stripe.com/api/subscriptions/object.md) objects. | Accept real credit cards and work with customer accounts. You can accept actual payment authorizations, charges, and captures for credit cards and accounts.
L45: | Disputes have a more nuanced flow and a simpler [testing process](https://docs.stripe.com/testing.md#disputes). Also, some [payment methods](https://docs.stripe.com/payments/payment-methods.md) have a more nuanced flow and require more steps. |
L46: ### API keys for autonomous agents
L47: 
L48: When you create a restricted API key, you can tag it as belonging to an autonomous agent, an AI system that operates independently to complete tasks such as processing refunds or managing subscriptions. To tag a key as an agent key, select **Authorizing agent access to your account** when Stripe prompts you for the key’s intended use during creation.
L49: 
L50: Agent-tagged keys work the same as other restricted API keys for authentication and permissions.
L51: The difference is in governance: agent-tagged keys are automatically subject to [approval rules](https://docs.stripe.com/account/approvals.md), which require a designated reviewer to approve sensitive actions before they take effect. Stripe provides a set of default rules when you create your first agent-tagged key. These rules cover high-risk actions such as payouts, refunds, and account configuration changes.
L52: This is the recommended way to give autonomous agents access to your Stripe account. The approval rules act as a safeguard against agent mistakes, unexpected behavior, and hallucinations—giving you visibility and control without blocking agents from doing their jobs.
L53: ## Protect your keys
L54: 
L55: Only publishable keys are safe to expose outside your application’s backend. You’re responsible for protecting other Stripe API keys, including restricted API keys. To protect your keys:
L56: - Store sensitive keys in a secrets vault provided by your hosting platform. [This blog post](https://stripe.dev/blog/securing-stripe-api-keys-aws-automatic-rotation) offers an example. If you can’t use a secrets vault, use environment variables to provide keys to your backend applications.
L57: - Don’t put keys in source code or configuration files checked into version control.
L58: - Configure [access policies](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#access-policies) so keys can only be used from your known servers.
L59: - [Rotate keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#rolling-keys) when team members with access to the keys leave your organization.
L60: - Don’t share keys over email, chat, or other unencrypted channels.
L61: For a comprehensive guide, see [best practices for managing secret API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md). We also maintain [a library of skills](https://github.com/stripe/ai/tree/main/skills) to help AI agents follow these best practices.
L62: ## Manage your API keys
L63: 
L64: The following sections describe how to create and manage keys on the API keys page.
L65: #### Create a restricted API key
L66: 
L67: Use [restricted API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/restricted-api-keys.md) (RAKs) for most use cases. You can use a RAK to assign the exact permissions your integration needs, which can help reduce the damage a fraudulent actor could cause to your business if they obtained your key.
L68: 
L69: - Follow the instructions on [Restricted API Keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/restricted-api-keys.md) to create a RAK, configure its permissions, and migrate from secret keys.
L70: #### Create a secret API key
L71: 
L72: Create an unrestricted secret API key only when your integration requires access to all Stripe APIs and resources without restriction. If a fraudulent actor obtains your secret key, they can harm your business. We recommend using RAKs instead.
L73: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/test/apikeys) page, click **Create secret key**.
L74: 2. In the dialog, enter the verification code that we send you by email or text message. If the dialog doesn’t continue automatically, click **Continue**.
L75: 3. Enter a name in the **Key name** field, then click **Create**.
L76: 4. Click the key value to copy it.
L77: 5. Save the key value. You can’t retrieve it later.
L78: 6. In the **Add a note** field, enter the location where you saved the key, then click **Done**.
L79: ### Reveal an API key
L80: When you create a secret key in live mode, Stripe displays it one time before you save it. Copy the key before you save it because you can’t reveal it later. We can’t recover keys that you’ve forgotten or lost access to. If you lose a key, rotate or delete it and create another. In live mode, you can reveal only API keys that Stripe creates for you, such as a default secret key or a key generated by a scheduled rotation.
L81: In sandbox mode, you can always see all of your API keys, including restricted and secret keys. Publishable API keys aren’t sensitive, so we show them by default and you don’t need to do anything to reveal them.
L82: > Store sensitive keys in a place where you won’t lose them, such as a secrets vault provided by your platform. Don’t put keys in your application’s code.
L83: 
L84: **Reveal a RAK in live mode**
L85: 
L86: You can reveal only live-mode RAKs that we created for you. If you create a RAK yourself, you can’t reveal it after you’ve seen it once.
L87: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys) page in live mode, in the **Restricted keys** list, click **Reveal live key** for the key you want to reveal.
L88: 2. Click the key value to copy it.
L89: 3. Save the key value in your platform’s [secrets vault](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md#use-a-secrets-vault). If your platform doesn’t provide one, use an environment variable.
L90: 4. Click **Hide live key**.
L91: 
L92: **Reveal a secret API key in live mode**
L93: You can reveal only live-mode secret keys that we created for you. If you create a secret key yourself, you can’t reveal it after you’ve seen it once.
L94: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys) page in live mode, in the **Standard keys** list, click **Reveal live key** for the key you want to reveal.
L95: 2. Click the key value to copy it.
L96: 3. Save the key value in your platform’s [secrets vault](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md#use-a-secrets-vault). If your platform doesn’t provide one, use an environment variable.
L97: 4. Click **Hide live key**.
L98: 5. Click the overflow menu (⋯), then select **Edit key** for the key you want to add a note to.
L99: 6. In the **Note** field, enter the location where you saved the key, then click **Save**.
L100: ### Limit an API key to certain IP addresses
L101: 
L102: [Access policies](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#access-policies) have replaced IP address restrictions. Use policies, not restrictions.
L103: ### Change an API key’s name or note
L104: 
L105: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/test/apikeys) page, click the overflow menu (⋯) for the key you want to change.
L106: 2. Select **Edit key**.
L107: 3. Do the following:
L108:    - To change the name, enter a new name in the **Key name** field.
L109:    - To change the note text, enter the new note text in the **Note** field.
L110: 4. Click **Save**.
L111: ### Expire an API key
L112: 
L113: If you expire a secret API key or a restricted API key, you must create a new one and update any code that uses the expired key. Code that uses the expired key can no longer make API calls.
L114: 
L115: > You can’t expire a publishable key.
L116: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/test/apikeys) page, in the **Restricted keys** or **Standard keys** list, click the overflow menu (⋯) for the key you want to expire.
L117: 2. Select **Expire key**.
L118: 3. In the dialog, click **Expire key**. If you no longer want to expire the key, click **Cancel**.
L119: ### Rotate an API key
L120: 
L121: Rotating an API key revokes it and generates a replacement key that’s ready to use immediately. You can also schedule an API key to rotate after a certain time. The replacement key is named as follows:
L122: 
L123: - The replacement publishable key name is always `Publishable key`.
L124: - The replacement secret key name is always `Secret key`.
L125: - The replacement restricted key name is the same as the rotated key.
L126: 
L127: You can rename a secret or restricted API key by editing the key.
L128: Rotate an API key in scenarios such as:
L129: 
L130: - If you lose a secret or restricted API key in live mode, and you can’t recover it from the Dashboard.
L131: - If a secret or restricted API key is compromised, and you need to revoke it to block any potentially malicious API requests that might use the key.
L132: - If a team member with access to the key leaves your organization or changes roles.
L133: - If your policy requires rotating keys at certain intervals.
L134: #### Rotate safely to avoid downtime
L135: 
L136: To avoid downtime during key rotation:
L137: 1. **Use the grace period**: When you rotate a key in the Dashboard, both the old and new keys work for up to 7 days. This lets you migrate gradually without downtime. If you need more than 7 days, create a new key manually, migrate to it, then expire the old one when you’re done.
L138: 2. **Roll out gradually**: If possible, use the new key from a small subset of your servers or services first, and watch your server logs for errors before deploying further.
L139: 3. **Monitor before revoking**: Before the old key expires, [check its request logs](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#view-request-logs), and expire it only after its request volume has been at zero for a few hours or days.
L140: #### Rotate an API key in the Dashboard
L141: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/test/apikeys) page, click the overflow menu (⋯) for the key you want to rotate.
L142: 2. Select **Rotate key**.
L143: 3. Select an expiration date from the **Expiration** dropdown. If you choose **Now**, the old key is deleted. If you specify a time, the remaining time until the key expires displays below the key name.
L144: 4. Click **Rotate API key**.
L145: 5. Click the key value to copy it.
L146: 6. Save the key value. You can’t retrieve it later.
L147: 7. In the **Add a note** field, enter the location where you saved the key, then click **Save** or **Done**.
L148: ### Restore an API key’s access
L149: 
L150: An API key might have its access limited if it hasn’t been used to create transfers, payouts, or update payout destinations for over 180 days. You can’t use a limited access key to create payouts and transfers or to create payout destinations. You can restore access to use the key normally or to perform a blocked action.
L151: #### Restore access for an API key
L152: 
L153: 1. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/test/apikeys) page, click the overflow menu (⋯) for the key you want to restore.
L154: 2. Select **Restore access**.
L155: 3. Click **Restore**.
L156: 
L157: ## View API request logs for a key
L158: 
L159: To [open the API request logs](https://docs.stripe.com/workbench/overview.md#request-logs), click the overflow menu (⋯) for any key, then select **View request logs**. Opening the logs redirects you to Workbench in the Stripe Dashboard.
L160: ## Switch to live mode
L161: 
L162: When you’re ready to accept real payments, use live mode API keys instead of sandbox (test) keys. On the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys) page, toggle from **sandbox mode** to **live mode**. The page now shows your live mode API keys.
L163: 
L164: > #### Complete go-live checklist
L165: >
L166: > Switching API keys is only one step. Review the full [go-live checklist](https://docs.stripe.com/get-started/checklist/go-live.md) to make sure your integration is production ready.
L167: ### Publishable keys (client-side)
L168: 
L169: Copy your **live mode publishable key** (starts with `pk_live_`) and replace the `pk_test_` key in your client-side code. It’s safe to embed this key in your code or apps.
L170: ### Restricted or secret API keys (server-side)
L171: 
L172: Server-side API keys are sensitive, so review our [best practices for managing secret API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md). We recommend generating [restricted API keys](https://docs.stripe.com/keys/restricted-api-keys.md) for your server-side code to limit the damage to your business if your keys are ever exposed or compromised.
L173: 1. Before you start using a live mode key in your backend application, remove any hardcoded API keys from your code. Instead, use a [secrets vault](https://docs.stripe.com/keys-best-practices.md#use-a-secrets-vault) to supply the sandbox key, and confirm that your application still works. If your platform doesn’t provide a secrets vault, you can use an environment variable.
L174: 2. [Reveal](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#reveal-an-api-key) and copy your **live mode keys** (which start with `rk_live_` or `sk_live_`). Store the key value securely in your server environment.
L175: 3. Configure your server environment to supply live mode keys instead of sandbox keys to your application.
L176: #### Webhook signing keys (server-side)
L177: 
L178: If you use webhooks, update each webhook endpoint’s URL and copy the new **signing secret** from the [Webhooks](https://dashboard.stripe.com/webhooks) section of the Dashboard.
L179: ## Access policies
L180: 
L181: You can restrict access to a key by attaching an access policy to it. If someone attempts a request using a key they can’t access, Stripe blocks the request and notifies you.
L182: 
L183: Stripe recommends configuring access policies on all live mode keys. That notifies you of any unauthorized access, so you can rotate the keys accordingly.
L184: You can manage access by assigning different policies to different keys. For example, you can distinguish between staging and production environments by assigning different policies to their respective keys.
L185: ### Access policy types
L186: 
L187: Stripe supports the following types of access policies:
L188: 
L189: - **IP addresses**: Restrict access to one or more specific IPv4 addresses or CIDR ranges. Use this approach if your servers have fixed IP addresses.
L190: - **Advanced**: Restrict access by Autonomous System Number (ASN), country, and common threat categories. If you’re dynamically scaling, you can provide access to your cloud provider using the ASN and country.
L191: An advanced access policy can use any combination of the following rules:
L192: - **ASNs to allow**: Requests from specified ASNs are allowed; all others are blocked.
L193: - **Countries**: Requests from specified countries are allowed; all others are blocked.
L194: - **Sources**: Requests from selected sources are blocked. You can select the following sources:
L195:   - **Anonymous VPNs**: Third-party VPN services sold for privacy and anonymity (not including corporate VPNs). Consider blocking these if you don’t use VPNs to access the Stripe API.
L196:   - **Public proxies**: Open proxy servers from public lists. Consider blocking these if you don’t use public proxies to access the Stripe API.
L197:   - **Residential proxies**: Proxies associated with residential ISPs. Consider blocking these if you don’t use residential ISPs to access the Stripe API.
L198:   - **Tor exit nodes**: Traffic from the Tor network. Consider blocking these if you don’t access the Stripe API over Tor.
L199: Selecting multiple rules combines them using AND logic. For example, if you allow ASN 16509 (Amazon), allow the United States, and block Tor exit nodes, then the policy only allows requests from AWS IPs in the US that are not known to be Tor exit nodes. It blocks all other requests.
L200: ### Create an access policy
L201: 
L202: To create an access policy, go to the [Access policies](https://dashboard.stripe.com/api-access-policies) page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
L203: 1. Click **+ Create policy**.
L204: 2. Enter a name (for example, “Production servers”) and an optional description.
L205: 3. Select **IP addresses** or **Advanced**.
L206: 4. Depending on the selected type, configure the policy:
L207:    - **IP addresses:** Enter one or more valid public IPv4 addresses or CIDR ranges. For example, `192.0.2.0/24` covers the range 192.0.2.0–192.0.2.255.
L208:    - **Advanced:** Specify any combination of ASNs to allow, countries to allow, and sources to block, as described in [Access policy types](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#access-policy-types).
L209: 5. Click **Next**.
L210: 6. Review the policy details, then click **Create policy**.
L211: 7. If prompted to authenticate, follow the on-screen instructions.
L212: If the creation succeeded, the new policy appears in the list.
L213: ### Apply or remove an access policy
L214: 
L215: To apply an access policy to an API key, go to the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys) page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
L216: 1. In the **Standard keys** or **Restricted keys** list, find the key you want to update and open its overflow menu (⋯).
L217: 2. Select **Manage access policy**.
L218: 3. In the **Access policy** dropdown, select the policy you want.
L219: 4. Review the details of the selected policy, then click **Save**.
L220: 5. If prompted to authenticate, follow the on-screen instructions.
L221: 
L222: To remove an access policy from a key, go to the [API keys](https://dashboard.stripe.com/apikeys) page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
L223: 1. In the **Standard keys** or **Restricted keys** list, find the key you want to update and open its overflow menu (⋯).
L224: 2. Select **Manage access policy**.
L225: 3. In the **Access policy** dropdown, select **None**.
L226: 4. Click **Save**.
L227: ### Update an access policy
L228: 
L229: To make changes to an access policy, go to the [Access policies](https://dashboard.stripe.com/api-access-policies) page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
L230: 1. Find the policy you want to change, and open its overflow menu (⋯).
L231: 2. Select **Edit policy**.
L232: 3. Update the policy options as described in [Create an access policy](https://docs.stripe.com/keys.md#create-an-access-policy), then click **Next**.
L233: 4. Review the policy details, then click **Save**.
L234: 5. If prompted to authenticate, follow the on-screen instructions.
L235: 
L236: When you update an access policy, the changes apply immediately to all API keys it’s assigned to.
L237: ### Delete an access policy
L238: 
L239: To delete an access policy, go to the [Access policies](https://dashboard.stripe.com/api-access-policies) page in your Dashboard and follow these steps:
L240: 
L241: 1. Find the policy you want to delete and open its overflow menu (⋯).
L242: 2. Select **Delete policy**.
L243: 3. Review the confirmation dialog to understand the impact, then click **Delete policy**.
L244: Deleting an access policy immediately removes it from all API keys it was applied to. Those keys allow requests from any source until you apply another policy to them.
